newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA SEES 1996/97 SUGAR CROP AT 2.37 MLN TONNES.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA SEES 1996/97 SUGAR CROP AT 2.37 MLN TONNES.

text.p: South Africa expected its 1996/97 sugar crop to be in the region of 2.37 million tonnes, an industry official said on Monday.

"We are on our way down and I would think we are probably going to be closer to 2.35 (million tonnes). The official figure as it stands at the moment is 2.37," South African Cane Growers' Association chief economist Brian Sugden told Reuters.

But even with the crop reduced from the previous estimate of 2.4 million tonnes, it will be the best in 12 years. The country produced only 1.67 million tonnes of sugar in the 1995/96 season (April-March).
South Africa was just emerging from five years of drought which cost the country's sugar industry millions of rands in lost revenue.
Sugden said the industry's August crop estimate was 22,126 million tonnes of sugar cane which would yield a raw sugar crop of 2.37 million tonnes.

A crop of 2.37 million tonnes would leave more than a million tonnes of sugar for export and the South African Sugar Association said last month it had sold virtually all this season's export surplus.
The association said last week it had already shipped more than 55 percent of sugar exports.
The main export markets remain in the Far East where South Africa has traditional long-term commitments with Japan and South Korea. Shipments to Japan this season total around 250,000 tonnes.
South Africa is also diversifying its exports this season with sales to Canada, Malaysia, Singapore, Philippines and China -- in addition to the U.S. where South Africa has an import quota.
Within Africa, the Sugar Association has also signed a deal with soft drink manufacturer Coca Cola to supply refined sugar to the company's East African bottling operations.
Sugden said the country's sugar mills were now crushing cane at full capacity and some might extend the crushing season into January.
"There were a couple of mills that were struggling a little bit but I think that most of them were now in full swing," he added.
